Research

Skin biology.
A wider perspective.

Our work connects epigenetic skin aging, skin–brain interaction and inflammatory skin disease with medical devices, energy-based technologies and objective assessment.

01

Epigenetic Skin Aging

Epigenetic Skin Aging

What molecular signals drive skin aging?

We study changes in DNA methylation, histone regulation and microRNAs associated with ultraviolet exposure and aging. Observations in human skin and dermal fibroblasts guide mechanistic studies of extracellular matrix remodeling and photoaging.

PhotoagingEpigeneticsmicroRNAExtracellular matrix

02

Skin–Brain Interaction

Skin–Brain Interaction

How far can a signal from the skin travel?

We investigate connections among cutaneous UV exposure, neurotransmitters, neuropeptides and brain function. Animal studies examine dopamine- and substance P-associated changes in memory and synaptic plasticity, helping define mechanisms of communication between the skin and the rest of the body.

03

Inflammatory Skin Disease

Inflammatory Skin Disease

What can immune-cell states reveal about disease?

Clinical unmet needs in atopic dermatitis and related inflammatory skin diseases guide our research. We use single-cell RNA sequencing and high-dimensional immune profiling to study peripheral immune cells in severe AD, connecting cell states and interactions with clinical phenotypes and potential therapeutic targets.

04

Medical Devices & EBD

Medical Devices & EBD

How does energy change skin—and how can we measure it?

We study ways to assess skin responses and treatment outcomes of energy-based devices (EBD) objectively. We connect clinical observations with 3D skin imaging and quantitative analysis, working with optical and engineering researchers to develop approaches to skin assessment.

Medicine, research & management

Principal investigator Dong Hun Lee holds MD, PhD and MBA degrees. His background in medicine, research and business administration informs a perspective on medical-device and EBD research that considers both clinical needs and the potential use of new technologies.
